title: Security Program Management and Oversight
intro:
Domain 5 is the management layer of security: the policies that say what the organisation expects, the risk process that decides where money and effort go, the contracts that bind vendors, the compliance and privacy obligations that regulators enforce, the audits that prove the controls actually work, and the training that turns staff into a defensive layer rather than the weakest link. It carries 20 percent of the exam, second only to Domain 4, and it is the domain where candidates with a purely technical background lose the most marks because the questions are about judgement, ordering, and vocabulary rather than commands.

For a learner heading into GRC (governance, risk and compliance) at a Nigerian bank or fintech this domain is the actual job description. A GRC analyst spends their week maintaining a risk register, chasing policy attestations, filling vendor questionnaires, preparing evidence for ISO 27001 or CBN examinations, and tracking phishing simulation results. A SOC analyst meets it from the other side: playbooks, change tickets, incident reporting timelines, and the awareness metrics that explain why the same three users keep clicking links. Where it is accurate, these notes map Security+ vocabulary onto ISO 27001, NIST CSF 2.0, the CBN Risk-Based Cybersecurity Framework and the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, so the exam terms become working knowledge rather than trivia.

Study approach: read each deep dive after Messer's video, then rebuild the key contrasts from memory. Policy versus standard versus procedure versus guideline. Owner versus controller versus processor versus custodian. Risk appetite versus tolerance. SLE, ARO and ALE. RTO versus RPO, MTTR versus MTBF. SLA versus MOU versus MSA versus SOW versus NDA versus BPA. Known versus unknown environment testing. Most Domain 5 questions are scenarios that hinge on one of these distinctions, so if you can explain each pair to a friend without notes, you are ready.

objectives.title: Summarize elements of effective security governance

videos.title: Security Policies
videos.summary: Messer explains the role of high-level security policies and walks through the common ones: information security, acceptable use, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, SDLC and change management.
videos.deepDive:
A security policy is a statement of management intent. It answers the question what does this organisation require and who is accountable, and it is deliberately written at a level that survives technology changes. Policies sit at the top of a governance hierarchy: policies say what, standards say how much (the measurable requirement), procedures say how (step by step), and guidelines offer recommended practice that is not mandatory. The exam loves this hierarchy, so anchor it: if a document can be broken, it is a policy or standard; if it can only be followed badly, it is a procedure; if ignoring it is allowed, it is a guideline.

Why do policies matter beyond paperwork? Three reasons. First, enforceability: HR cannot discipline an employee for sharing a password unless a policy the employee acknowledged says not to. Second, accountability: a policy names an owner (usually the CISO or a board committee) so that when an auditor asks who approved this, there is an answer. Third, auditability: ISO 27001 clause 5.2 requires a documented information security policy approved by top management, and NIST CSF 2.0 put governance into its own function, Govern, precisely because policies are the evidence that leadership is steering the programme. The CBN Risk-Based Cybersecurity Framework similarly expects a board-approved cybersecurity policy and strategy reviewed at defined intervals.

The core policies you must recognise:

  • Information security policy: the umbrella. Scope, objectives, roles, and the statement that all other security documents derive authority from it.
  • Acceptable use policy (AUP): what users may and may not do with company systems, email, internet and devices. Signed at onboarding. Sample clause: Users must not connect personally owned storage devices to corporate endpoints without written approval from Information Security.
  • Business continuity (BC) policy: how critical business functions keep running during disruption, driven by a business impact analysis.
  • Disaster recovery (DR) policy: the IT-focused subset of BC, covering restoration of systems and data, alternate sites, and recovery objectives.
  • Incident response (IR) policy: authority to declare an incident, the response team, severity levels and mandatory reporting timelines (for a Nigerian bank this includes CBN incident reporting and the 72-hour breach notification to the Nigeria Data Protection Commission under the NDPA 2023).
  • Software development lifecycle (SDLC) policy: security gates at each phase: threat modelling, code review, testing, secure deployment.
  • Change management policy: no production change without an approved, documented, tested and reversible change request.

A useful contrast: a policy says all production changes require approval from the Change Advisory Board; the standard says emergency changes must be approved by two named authorities and documented within 24 hours; the procedure is the ticket workflow in ServiceNow or Jira. As a GRC analyst your job is to keep these aligned, track the annual review date of each policy, and collect the acknowledgement records that prove staff have read them.

keyTerms.def: A high-level, management-approved statement of what the organisation requires for security and who is accountable.
A policy defining permitted and prohibited uses of organisational systems, data and networks, acknowledged by every user.
Governs how critical business functions continue during and after a disruption.
The IT-focused part of continuity that governs restoring systems and data after a disaster.
Defines authority, roles, severity levels and reporting obligations for handling security incidents.
Requires security activities at each phase of software development, from design through deployment and retirement.
Requires that changes to production systems be requested, approved, tested, documented and reversible.
Recommended, non-mandatory practice that supports policies and standards.

examTips: If a question asks for the document that states management intent at the highest level, the answer is a policy, not a standard or procedure.
AUP questions usually describe an employee doing something with company equipment; the fix is enforcing or updating the AUP.
Distinguish BC (keep the business running) from DR (restore the IT systems); DR is a subset of BC.
Change management appears in almost every domain; in 5.1 it is the policy, in 1.3 it is the process and impacts.
videos.realWorld: In a Nigerian bank the GRC team owns a policy register: each policy has an owner, a version, an approval date and a next review date, and the ISO 27001 auditor will ask for it in the first hour. New hires sign the AUP through the HR system, and the signed record is what Information Security produces when an insider incident goes to a disciplinary panel. When the CBN examiners visit, the board-approved cybersecurity policy and evidence of its periodic review are among the first items requested.

quiz.q: A fintech is preparing for its first ISO 27001 certification audit. The auditor asks for the document that shows top management has defined the organisation's overall security direction and accountability. Which document satisfies this request?
quiz.explain: The information security policy is the top-level, management-approved statement of intent and accountability. A standard defines measurable requirements, a playbook is a procedure, and a guideline is optional guidance.

quiz.q: An employee is found to have installed a cryptocurrency miner on a company laptop. HR wants to take disciplinary action but the employee claims no rule was ever communicated. Which document would the security team most need to produce?
quiz.explain: The AUP defines what users may and may not do with company equipment and is acknowledged at onboarding. The signed acknowledgement proves the rule was communicated. The other documents do not govern individual user conduct.

quiz.q: After a data centre flood, a payments company needs a document that defines how quickly core banking systems must be restored and at which alternate site. Which policy governs this?
quiz.explain: Restoring IT systems and data after a disaster, including alternate sites and recovery objectives, is disaster recovery. Business continuity is broader, incident response covers handling security events, and SDLC covers software development.

videos.title: Security Standards
videos.summary: Messer covers how standards make policies measurable, using password, access control, physical security and encryption standards as examples.
videos.deepDive:
A standard converts a policy into something you can test. The policy says authentication must be strong; the standard says passwords must be at least 14 characters, MFA is required for all remote and privileged access, and accounts lock after 5 failed attempts within 15 minutes. Because a standard is specific and mandatory, an auditor can sample 25 accounts and count how many comply. That is the whole point: policies give direction, standards give measurability, and without standards a policy is unenforceable good intentions.

Standards can be internal (written by your own security team) or external (adopted from a recognised body). Common external ones you will meet in a bank: ISO/IEC 27001 (the management system) and ISO/IEC 27002 (the control catalogue behind Annex A), PCI DSS for cardholder data, NIST SP 800-63B for digital identity and passwords, and the CBN Risk-Based Cybersecurity Framework, which in practice acts as a mandatory external standard for Nigerian deposit money banks and payment service providers. Organisations usually write internal standards that map to these so that one set of controls satisfies several obligations at once.

The four standards Security+ names explicitly:

  • Password standard: length, complexity or passphrase rules, history, maximum age (modern guidance from NIST 800-63B drops forced periodic rotation unless compromise is suspected), lockout thresholds, storage (salted hashing with bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2), and prohibited passwords checked against breach lists.
  • Access control standard: how access is requested, approved and reviewed. It typically mandates least privilege, role-based access, segregation of duties (the person who creates a payment cannot approve it), quarterly access recertification, and removal of access within a defined time after termination.
  • Physical security standard: badge access zones, visitor escort rules, CCTV retention periods, mantrap or vestibule use for data centres, clean desk requirements and secure disposal of media.
  • Encryption standard: approved algorithms and key lengths (AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.2 or higher in transit, RSA 2048 or ECC P-256 minimum for keys), approved key management practices (rotation intervals, HSM use for signing keys, split knowledge for master keys), and a list of deprecated algorithms such as DES, RC4, MD5 and SHA-1 that must not be used.

Worked example: a fintech policy states that customer data must be protected in transit and at rest. The encryption standard then reads: All databases containing customer PII must use transparent data encryption with AES-256. TLS 1.3 is required for all external APIs; TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are prohibited. Encryption keys must be stored in the approved KMS and rotated every 12 months. The GRC analyst now has three things to check, and the SOC can write a detection for any service still negotiating TLS 1.0.

Standards should be versioned and reviewed on a schedule, because cryptography ages: a standard written in 2015 that permits SHA-1 certificates is a finding today. When a standard cannot be met by a legacy system, the answer is a formal exception with a compensating control and an expiry date, which you will meet again in risk management strategies.

keyTerms.def: A mandatory, specific and measurable requirement that implements a policy, such as minimum password length.
Defines length, complexity, history, lockout, storage and prohibited-password rules for authentication credentials.
Defines how access is requested, approved, reviewed and revoked, usually enforcing least privilege and segregation of duties.
Defines requirements for badges, visitor handling, CCTV, data centre entry and media disposal.
Lists approved algorithms, key lengths, protocols and key management practices and prohibits deprecated ones.
Splitting a sensitive task between two people so no single person can complete it alone.
A documented, time-limited approval to deviate from a standard, normally paired with a compensating control.

examTips: A question that contains specific numbers (character counts, key lengths, retention days) is describing a standard, not a policy.
If a legacy system cannot meet the encryption standard, the exam answer is usually a documented exception plus a compensating control, not ignoring the standard.
Know the mapping: policy is the what, standard is the measurable how much, procedure is the how, guideline is optional.
videos.realWorld: Bank GRC teams keep a control library where each internal standard is mapped to ISO 27001 Annex A controls, PCI DSS requirements and CBN framework clauses, so one piece of evidence (for example the quarterly access review export) can be reused across three audits. SOC analysts consume standards as detection logic: the encryption standard becomes a rule that flags TLS 1.0 handshakes, and the access control standard becomes an alert when a privileged group gains a new member outside the change window.

quiz.q: A bank's information security policy states that access to customer data must be limited to those with a business need. Which document would specify that access reviews occur quarterly and that terminated staff must lose access within 24 hours?
quiz.explain: Specific, measurable requirements such as review frequency and revocation timelines belong in a standard. The AUP governs user behaviour, a procedure gives step-by-step instructions, and a guideline is not mandatory.

quiz.q: During an assessment, an analyst finds a payment gateway still accepting TLS 1.0 connections. Which document would the analyst cite to classify this as non-compliant?
quiz.explain: The encryption standard lists approved and prohibited protocols and algorithms. TLS 1.0 is deprecated, so accepting it violates the standard. The other documents do not define cryptographic requirements.

quiz.q: A core banking application cannot support 14-character passwords required by the password standard, and the vendor will not patch it for six months. What is the most appropriate governance action?
options: Ignore the requirement since the vendor is at fault
Approve a documented, time-limited exception with a compensating control such as MFA
Disconnect the core banking application until it complies
Rewrite the password standard to allow 8 characters for everyone
quiz.explain: A formal exception with a compensating control and an expiry date maintains governance while acknowledging reality. Weakening the standard for everyone increases risk, ignoring it removes accountability, and disconnecting core banking is disproportionate.

videos.title: Security Procedures
videos.summary: Messer explains procedures as the step-by-step operational documents, covering change management, onboarding and offboarding, and playbooks, plus the need for monitoring and revision.
videos.deepDive:
A procedure is the document a person follows at 2 a.m. when they are tired and the thing has to be done right. Where a policy expresses intent and a standard sets a measurable bar, a procedure is a numbered list of steps with named roles, inputs, outputs and decision points. Good procedures are boringly explicit: they name the ticket system, the approval group, the command to run, the evidence to attach, and what to do if a step fails. That precision is why procedures are what you actually test during an audit walkthrough.

The three procedure families Security+ names:

  1. Change management procedure: how a change moves from request to closure. Typical steps: raise a change record with description, business justification and risk rating; complete an impact analysis listing affected systems and dependencies; attach a test plan and results from a non-production environment; attach a backout plan; obtain Change Advisory Board (CAB) approval or, for standard low-risk changes, pre-approval; schedule inside the maintenance window; implement; verify; update the configuration management database; close the record. Emergency changes follow a shortened path but must still be documented afterwards. Auditors sample closed changes and check every artefact exists.
  2. Onboarding and offboarding procedures: onboarding creates identity and access in the right order: HR record, background check, AUP and NDA signature, security awareness training completion, account creation from an approved role template, hardware issue with asset tag recorded. Offboarding is the mirror image and is the one that gets forgotten: HR trigger, disable accounts (do not delete immediately, since mailbox and file access may be needed), revoke tokens and VPN certificates, collect devices and badges, rotate any shared credentials the person knew, transfer data ownership, and record completion. The classic exam failure is the ex-employee whose VPN still works three months later.
  3. Playbooks: procedures for specific security events. A phishing playbook, for example: triage the reported email, extract indicators (sender, URL, attachment hash), check whether other users received it, search the mail gateway and purge, block indicators on proxy and EDR, check whether anyone clicked or entered credentials, reset affected passwords and revoke sessions, notify users, record the incident, and update the awareness metrics. Playbooks are what SOC analysts live in, and platforms like SOAR tools automate their repeatable parts.

Two supporting ideas matter. Governance structures decide who approves what: a board or its risk committee approves policies, a security steering committee approves standards, and operational managers own procedures. In a centralised model one security function writes and enforces everything for the whole group; in a decentralised model each business unit or subsidiary runs its own, with the centre setting minimum requirements. Large Nigerian bank holding companies are often hybrid: group sets policy, each subsidiary runs procedures. Government entities such as the CBN, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and NITDA sit outside the organisation but shape what the policies must contain.

Monitoring and revision is the discipline that stops documents rotting. Every policy, standard and procedure carries a review date, typically annual, plus event-driven triggers: a new regulation, a major incident, an audit finding, a reorganisation or a technology change. A procedure that references a decommissioned ticketing tool is an audit finding waiting to happen, so the GRC calendar tracks review dates just like patch cycles.

keyTerms.def: A step-by-step operational document describing exactly how a task is performed, by whom and with what evidence.
The workflow for requesting, assessing, approving, testing, implementing, verifying and documenting a change.
Documented steps to reverse a change and restore the prior state if implementation fails.
The procedure for bringing a new user in: agreements, training, identity creation and access provisioning.
The procedure for removing a departing user: disabling accounts, revoking access, collecting assets and rotating shared secrets.
A predefined, repeatable set of response steps for a specific type of security event, such as phishing or ransomware.
A single security function sets and enforces policy for the whole organisation.
Individual business units manage their own security programmes within minimum requirements set centrally.

examTips: Playbook questions usually describe a repeatable incident type and ask what will make response faster and more consistent.
Offboarding scenarios almost always hinge on access that was not revoked; the answer involves the offboarding procedure or disabling accounts promptly.
If a scenario mentions a board committee versus business unit heads making security decisions, it is testing centralised versus decentralised governance.
Policies must be reviewed on a schedule and after triggering events; the exam calls this monitoring and revision.
videos.realWorld: In a SOC the playbook library is the team's memory: a tier-1 analyst who has never seen a business email compromise can still handle one correctly by following the BEC playbook, and the SOAR platform runs the enrichment and blocking steps automatically. On the GRC side, the offboarding procedure is a recurring ISO 27001 and CBN examination sample: auditors take the HR leavers list for the quarter and check the date each account was disabled, and any gap over the standard's limit becomes a finding.

quiz.q: A SOC team notices that different analysts handle phishing reports inconsistently, with some forgetting to check whether other mailboxes received the same message. What should the team implement to fix this?
quiz.explain: A playbook provides a repeatable, step-by-step response for a specific event type, ensuring every analyst performs the same checks. Policies and standards do not give operational steps, and governance models do not address response consistency.

quiz.q: Three months after a contractor's engagement ended, logs show their VPN account authenticating successfully. Which governance element most likely failed?
quiz.explain: Offboarding is responsible for disabling accounts and revoking access when a person leaves. A working VPN account months later indicates the offboarding steps were not completed. The other documents do not govern access removal.

quiz.q: A bank holding company sets minimum security requirements at group level, but each subsidiary's IT team writes and runs its own operational procedures and approves its own low-risk changes. Which governance structure does this describe?
quiz.explain: Business units running their own procedures within centrally defined minimums is a decentralised (or hybrid) structure. Fully centralised would have one function doing everything; government entities influence but do not run internal governance.

videos.title: Security Considerations
videos.summary: Messer discusses the external factors that shape a security programme: regulatory, legal, industry, and local, regional, national and global considerations.
videos.deepDive:
No security programme is designed in a vacuum. External considerations are the forces outside the organisation that dictate what the policies must contain, and a GRC analyst's first task on any new requirement is to ask which external obligation drives this, and what happens if we miss it. Security+ groups these into regulatory, legal, industry and geographic considerations, and the exam tests whether you can identify which one a scenario describes.

Regulatory considerations come from bodies with the legal power to supervise a sector. For a Nigerian bank the Central Bank of Nigeria is the primary regulator, and its Risk-Based Cybersecurity Framework and Guidelines for Deposit Money Banks and Payment Service Banks sets expectations such as board-level cyber oversight, a designated CISO, risk assessments, incident reporting to the CBN, and regular vulnerability assessments and penetration testing. Fintechs holding CBN licences (payment service providers, mobile money operators, switching companies) fall under related guidelines. The Nigeria Data Protection Commission, created by the NDPA 2023, regulates personal data. The Securities and Exchange Commission regulates capital market operators. Regulators can fine, restrict operations or revoke licences, which is why regulatory requirements always rank at the top of the priority list.

Legal considerations are statutes and case law that apply regardless of sector: the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015, as amended in 2024, criminalises unauthorised access and mandates certain reporting; the NDPA 2023 creates data subject rights and breach notification duties; evidence preservation rules affect how incidents must be documented if litigation follows. Contract law also belongs here: an SLA breach with a customer is a legal exposure even when no regulator is involved.

Industry considerations are obligations that come from the market rather than from law. PCI DSS is the classic example: it is a contractual standard imposed by the card brands through acquiring banks, not a statute, yet failing it can end your ability to process cards. SWIFT's Customer Security Programme is another, with annual attestation required of every SWIFT-connected bank. ISO 27001 certification is voluntary but often demanded by enterprise customers before they sign.

Geographic considerations scale from local to global. Local: Lagos State or municipal rules on physical premises and CCTV. Regional: ECOWAS data harmonisation efforts, or for a company with EU customers the GDPR's extraterritorial reach. National: Nigerian data localisation expectations, such as CBN guidance on where certain financial data may be hosted and NITDA's cloud and data residency guidelines. Global: cross-border data transfer restrictions, sanctions lists (OFAC, UN), and the reality that a fintech serving diaspora remittances must satisfy the regulator in every jurisdiction it operates in, not only Nigeria.

Worked example: a Lagos fintech launches a card product for customers in Nigeria and Ghana. Its GRC team must satisfy the CBN (regulatory, national), the Bank of Ghana (regulatory, regional), PCI DSS (industry), the NDPA and Ghana's Data Protection Act (legal), and if it stores data in a European cloud region, the GDPR transfer rules (global). One control set, five external drivers, and a compliance matrix that shows which control satisfies which obligation.

keyTerms.def: A requirement imposed by a government body with supervisory power over a sector, such as the CBN for banks.
A statutory or contractual obligation that applies regardless of industry, such as data protection law or cybercrime law.
A requirement imposed by the market or trade bodies rather than by law, such as PCI DSS or SWIFT CSP.
A requirement that certain data be stored or processed within a specific country's borders.
A law that applies to organisations outside the enacting country because they serve its residents, such as GDPR.
A mapping of controls to every external obligation they satisfy, used to avoid duplicate work across audits.
CBN guidelines requiring Nigerian banks and payment providers to implement board-governed cybersecurity programmes with defined reporting and testing.

examTips: PCI DSS is an industry standard, not a law. If a question calls it a regulatory requirement, that option is a distractor.
When a scenario spans multiple countries, look for the option about global or regional legal considerations and data transfer rules.
Regulatory failures carry the harshest consequence on the exam: loss of licence. Legal failures bring fines and lawsuits; industry failures bring contractual penalties.
videos.realWorld: A GRC analyst at a Nigerian fintech maintains a regulatory obligations register listing each applicable requirement (CBN framework clauses, NDPA articles, PCI DSS requirements, SWIFT CSP controls), its owner, the evidence needed and the next due date. When the CBN issues a new circular, the analyst performs a gap assessment against that register within days, because CBN circulars often carry compliance deadlines and the bank's licence is the ultimate consequence.

quiz.q: A Nigerian fintech processes card payments and must comply with PCI DSS as a condition of its acquiring bank relationship. Which category of external consideration does PCI DSS represent?
quiz.explain: PCI DSS is imposed by the card brands through contractual relationships, making it an industry consideration. It is not a statute (legal) and not enforced by a government regulator (regulatory).

quiz.q: A bank plans to host customer transaction data in a cloud region outside Nigeria. Which external consideration should the GRC team evaluate first?
options: The vendor's marketing claims about uptime
Industry best practice for cloud architecture
National data localisation and regulator hosting requirements
Local building codes for the data centre
quiz.explain: Hosting financial data abroad raises national regulatory and legal questions about data residency and the regulator's expectations. Building codes and marketing claims are irrelevant to the core issue, and best practice is secondary to legal permissibility.

quiz.q: A remittance startup in Lagos serves customers in the United Kingdom. Its security team is told it must handle data subject requests under both the NDPA 2023 and UK GDPR. Which type of consideration explains why a foreign law applies?
options: Global legal considerations with extraterritorial reach
quiz.explain: Laws such as UK GDPR apply to organisations outside the country when they serve its residents, which is a global legal consideration. The CBN does not issue regional guidance for the UK, and municipal rules or industry standards do not create this obligation.

videos.title: Data Roles and Responsibilities
videos.summary: Messer defines the key data governance roles: owners, controllers, processors, and custodians or stewards, and explains what each is responsible for.
videos.deepDive:
Data governance assigns named people to named responsibilities so that when something goes wrong there is no shrug. Security+ tests four roles, and two of them (controller and processor) come straight from data protection law, so the definitions must be precise.

Data owner: the senior business person accountable for a data set. Not IT. The owner decides the classification (public, internal, confidential, restricted), who may access it, how long it is kept and what controls are acceptable. In a bank the Head of Retail Banking might own customer account data, the CFO owns financial reporting data, the Head of HR owns employee records. Owners sign off on access reviews and risk acceptance for their data. The exam trick: the owner is accountable even though they never touch a server.

Data custodian or steward: the person or team that implements the owner's decisions day to day. Custodians are usually IT or database teams: they apply the access control lists, run backups, apply encryption, monitor logs, and enforce retention. Some organisations split the terms: a steward focuses on data quality, metadata and correct usage, while a custodian focuses on technical protection. For the exam treat them as the operational role that carries out the owner's instructions and is responsible (not accountable) for protection.

Data controller: the organisation (a legal entity, not a person) that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. Under the NDPA 2023, as under GDPR, the controller carries the primary legal obligations: lawful basis, transparency, data subject rights, breach notification to the Nigeria Data Protection Commission within 72 hours, and, for controllers of major importance, registration with the NDPC and appointment of a Data Protection Officer.

Data processor: an organisation that processes personal data on behalf of and on the instructions of a controller. A cloud provider hosting the bank's CRM, a payroll bureau, an SMS gateway sending OTPs, a BPO handling call-centre overflow. Processors must act only on documented instructions, keep the data secure, assist the controller with data subject requests and breaches, and not engage sub-processors without approval. The contract between them is a data processing agreement.

Worked example: a large commercial bank (controller) uses a Lagos fintech to run its loyalty rewards app. The fintech is a processor. The bank's Head of Cards is the data owner for the loyalty data set. The fintech's platform engineers and the bank's database administrators are custodians. If the fintech suffers a breach, it must notify the bank promptly; the bank, as controller, must notify the NDPC and affected customers. If the fintech started using the loyalty data to market its own products, it would be deciding purposes itself and would become a controller for that use, taking on the full legal liability.

A quick contrast to lock in: owner and custodian are internal governance roles about accountability versus execution; controller and processor are legal roles about who decides versus who follows instructions. A single organisation is usually both a controller (for its own customer data) and a processor (when it handles data for partners). The data subject, the living person the data is about, is never one of the four roles but is the reason the roles exist, and you will meet their rights again in 5.4.

keyTerms.def: The senior business role accountable for a data set, deciding its classification, access and retention.
The technical role responsible for implementing the owner's decisions: access controls, backups, encryption and monitoring.
A role focused on data quality, definitions and appropriate use, often overlapping with custodian.
The organisation that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data and carries primary legal liability.
An organisation that processes personal data on behalf of a controller and only on its documented instructions.
The identifiable living person to whom personal data relates.
The designated person who oversees a controller's or processor's compliance with data protection law.
The contract between a controller and processor defining instructions, security, sub-processing and breach duties.

examTips: Owner is accountable, custodian is responsible. If the question asks who classifies data or approves access, it is the owner; if it asks who applies the permissions or runs backups, it is the custodian.
Controller decides why and how personal data is processed; processor acts on instructions. A vendor that starts using data for its own purposes becomes a controller.
Do not confuse system owner (responsible for a system) with data owner (accountable for a data set); the exam prefers data owner for classification questions.
videos.realWorld: A GRC analyst keeps a data inventory that lists each data set, its owner, its custodian, its classification and whether the bank is controller or processor for it. That inventory drives the annual access recertification, where each owner must confirm every user of their data still needs it, and it is the first document the DPO opens when a data subject access request or a breach arrives, because it shows exactly who must be involved and which processors must be contacted.

quiz.q: A bank's Head of Retail Banking decides that customer account data is classified as Restricted and that only branch staff and the fraud team may access it. The database team applies the permissions. Which role does the Head of Retail Banking hold?
quiz.explain: Deciding classification and who may access a data set is the data owner's accountability. The database team applying permissions is the custodian. Processors act for controllers, and the data subject is the customer.

quiz.q: A Lagos fintech sends OTP SMS messages to a bank's customers using phone numbers supplied by the bank and only as instructed by the bank. Under the NDPA 2023, what is the fintech's role?
quiz.explain: The fintech processes personal data on behalf of and on the instructions of the bank, which decides the purpose. That makes the fintech a processor and the bank the controller.

quiz.q: A payroll provider that processes employee data for several companies begins using the aggregated salary data to sell market benchmarking reports without the companies' instruction. How does this change its role?
options: It remains a processor because it already had the data
It becomes a data controller for that new processing and takes on controller liability
quiz.explain: By deciding its own purpose for the data, the provider is now determining purposes and means, which is the definition of a controller. It therefore carries controller obligations for that processing, including lawful basis and data subject rights.

objectives.title: Explain elements of the risk management process

videos.title: Risk Management
videos.summary: Messer introduces risk identification and the different cadences of risk assessment: ad hoc, recurring, one-time and continuous.
videos.deepDive:
Risk management is the process that decides where a finite security budget goes. Every organisation faces more threats than it can fund defences against, so it needs a repeatable way to find risks, size them, decide what to do about each, and prove to the board and regulators that the decision was deliberate. Security+ frames the process as identification, assessment, analysis, treatment (the strategies) and reporting, which mirrors ISO 31000, ISO 27005 and NIST SP 800-30. ISO 27001 clause 6.1 requires a documented risk assessment and treatment process, and the CBN framework requires banks to run a cyber risk assessment and present results to the board, so this is not academic: it is what a GRC analyst maintains.

Risk identification is the discovery step. Sources include asset inventories (you cannot protect what you do not know you own), threat intelligence, vulnerability scan results, audit findings, incident history, vendor assessments, business change (a new mobile app, a new cloud region) and interviews with process owners. A risk statement is written so it can be assessed: not ransomware but a ransomware infection on the branch file server, via a phishing attachment, causes multi-day loss of branch operations and possible regulator reporting. Threat, vulnerability, asset and impact are all present in that sentence.

Risk assessment cadence is tested directly, so know the four terms:

  • Ad hoc: triggered by an event or a question. A new zero-day is announced, a merger is proposed, an executive asks whether the bank is exposed to a breach in the news. Quick, focused, unscheduled.
  • Recurring: scheduled at fixed intervals. The annual enterprise risk assessment, the quarterly review of the top 20 risks, the yearly ISO 27001 reassessment. Regulators usually expect at least annual.
  • One-time: performed once for a specific project or change and not repeated. A risk assessment before launching a new USSD banking channel, or before migrating core banking to a new data centre. Its output feeds the change or project approval.
  • Continuous: ongoing, tool-driven assessment that updates risk posture in near real time: vulnerability management platforms, attack surface monitoring, cloud security posture management, and key risk indicators fed from the SIEM. NIST CSF 2.0 and modern GRC platforms push organisations toward this model.

A mature programme uses all four: continuous monitoring for technical exposure, recurring reviews for governance, one-time assessments for projects, and ad hoc responses to events.

Worked example of a risk register row (the register itself is explained in the next video, but the shape matters here): R-014 | Phishing leads to compromise of a treasury officer's email and fraudulent SWIFT instruction | Owner: Head of Treasury | Likelihood: 4/5 | Impact: 5/5 | Inherent score: 20 | Controls: MFA, payment dual authorisation, DMARC, awareness | Residual: 2 x 5 = 10 | Treatment: mitigate, target 5 by Q4 | KRI: phishing click rate above 5 percent. Every part of the Security+ vocabulary lives in that one line.

The distinction that trips candidates: risk management is the whole cycle; risk assessment is the step of finding and sizing risks; risk analysis is the specific technique (qualitative or quantitative) used to size them. Keep those nested and the scenario questions resolve themselves.

keyTerms.def: The end-to-end process of identifying, assessing, treating, monitoring and reporting risk to keep it within acceptable bounds.
Discovering and documenting risks from asset inventories, threat intelligence, scans, audits, incidents and business change.
The step of evaluating identified risks for likelihood and impact to decide their significance.
An unscheduled assessment triggered by a specific event, question or new threat.
An assessment repeated on a fixed schedule such as quarterly or annually.
An assessment performed once for a specific project or change and not repeated.
Ongoing, usually automated assessment that updates risk posture in near real time.
A sentence linking a threat, a vulnerability, an asset and a consequence so the risk can be assessed.

examTips: Match the cadence to the trigger: event or question equals ad hoc, schedule equals recurring, project equals one-time, automated and ongoing equals continuous.
Risk identification comes before assessment; if a scenario has no asset inventory yet, the first step is identification, not analysis.
Regulator-driven annual risk assessments are recurring, even if the organisation only started doing them because of a rule.
videos.realWorld: A junior GRC analyst at a bank typically inherits the enterprise risk register and runs the recurring cycle: sending risk owners their quarterly review, collecting evidence that controls still operate, updating scores, and preparing the risk committee pack. When a widely reported vulnerability lands, the analyst runs an ad hoc assessment with the vulnerability management team within 48 hours and briefs the CISO, because the board will ask and the CBN may issue a circular demanding a response.

quiz.q: A critical vulnerability in a widely used VPN appliance is announced on a Friday evening. The CISO asks the GRC team to determine by Monday whether the bank is exposed and what the impact would be. Which type of risk assessment is this?
quiz.explain: An assessment triggered by a specific unplanned event or question is ad hoc. Recurring is scheduled, one-time is tied to a defined project, and continuous is ongoing automated monitoring.

quiz.q: A fintech is about to launch a new agent banking platform and performs a risk assessment as part of the go-live approval. It has no plan to repeat this specific assessment. Which cadence does this describe?
quiz.explain: A single assessment tied to a specific project or change, not repeated afterwards, is one-time. It is planned (so not ad hoc) and not scheduled to repeat (so not recurring).

quiz.q: A bank's board requires an enterprise cyber risk assessment every year as mandated by its regulator, and the SOC also feeds vulnerability scan results into a dashboard that updates risk scores daily. Which two cadences are in use?
quiz.explain: The annual mandated assessment is recurring, and the daily automated scoring from scan data is continuous. Neither is tied to a single project or an unplanned trigger.

videos.title: Risk Analysis
videos.summary: Messer explains qualitative and quantitative analysis, the SLE, ARO and ALE formulas, exposure factor, likelihood versus probability, and the risk register with key risk indicators, owners and thresholds.
videos.deepDive:
Risk analysis is how you turn a worry into a number or a ranking so that risks can be compared and prioritised. Two approaches exist and the exam expects you to know when each fits and how to compute the quantitative one.

Qualitative analysis uses descriptive scales. Likelihood is rated (for example 1 Rare to 5 Almost certain) and impact is rated (1 Negligible to 5 Severe), and the product or a heat map position gives a risk level. It is fast, needs little data, and works for reputational or regulatory harm that resists monetary valuation. Its weakness is subjectivity: two managers will rate the same risk differently unless the scales have clear definitions, so good programmes define each level (Impact 5 means regulator sanction, loss above N500 million, or customer-facing outage over 24 hours).

Quantitative analysis assigns money. The Security+ formulas:

  • Asset value (AV): what the asset is worth, including replacement and revenue it supports.
  • Exposure factor (EF): the fraction of the asset's value lost in a single event, expressed as a percentage.
  • Single loss expectancy (SLE) = AV x EF. The cost of one occurrence.
  • Annualised rate of occurrence (ARO): how many times per year the event is expected. Once every four years is 0.25.
  • Annualised loss expectancy (ALE) = SLE x ARO. The expected yearly cost of the risk.

Worked example. A fintech's card processing platform generates N800 million in annual revenue and its data and infrastructure are valued at N400 million. A successful ransomware attack is estimated to destroy or lock 30 percent of that value (EF = 0.30) before recovery. SLE = N400 million x 0.30 = N120 million. Threat intelligence and the firm's own history suggest such an event once every five years, so ARO = 0.2. ALE = N120 million x 0.2 = N24 million per year. A proposed EDR and immutable backup programme costs N15 million a year and is expected to cut ARO to 0.05 and EF to 10 percent. New SLE = N40 million, new ALE = N2 million. Annual benefit = N24 million minus N2 million = N22 million, against a N15 million cost, so the control is justified. That cost-benefit comparison (ALE before minus ALE after minus cost of control) is exactly what the exam expects you to reason through.

Probability versus likelihood: probability is a mathematical measure (0 to 1 or a percentage) usually backed by data; likelihood is the broader, often qualitative estimate of chance used when data is thin. Exam questions treat them as near-synonyms but may present likelihood as the qualitative term and probability as the quantitative one. Impact is the magnitude of harm: financial, operational, regulatory, reputational, or to life and safety.

The risk register is the living document that holds all this. Each row carries a description, category, owner, inherent likelihood and impact, existing controls, residual score, treatment decision, target date and status. Three fields are tested by name:

  • Risk owner: the person accountable for managing that risk and reporting on it. Always a business or senior role, never the GRC analyst who maintains the register.
  • Key risk indicators (KRIs): measurable early-warning metrics. Phishing click rate, percentage of critical patches over 30 days old, number of privileged accounts without MFA, unresolved high-severity audit findings.
  • Risk threshold: the level at which a risk or KRI must be escalated or acted upon. A patch KRI threshold of 5 percent means anything above triggers action.

Two further terms: risk tolerance is how much variation from the desired risk level the organisation will bear for a given risk; risk appetite is the overall amount of risk the organisation is willing to pursue to meet its goals, and the next video expands it.

keyTerms.def: Rating likelihood and impact on descriptive scales such as low, medium and high to rank risks without monetary values.
Assigning monetary values to assets, losses and frequencies to calculate expected loss.
The percentage of an asset's value lost in a single occurrence of a risk event.
The cost of one occurrence of a risk event, calculated as asset value multiplied by exposure factor.
The expected number of times a risk event occurs in one year.
The expected yearly cost of a risk, calculated as SLE multiplied by ARO.
The document listing identified risks with owners, scores, controls, treatments and status.
A measurable metric that provides early warning that a risk is increasing.
The defined level at which a risk or indicator triggers escalation or action.
The accountable individual responsible for managing and reporting on a specific risk.

examTips: Memorise SLE = AV x EF and ALE = SLE x ARO; the exam will give you three of the four values and ask for the missing one.
ARO for an event every N years is 1 divided by N; every 4 years is 0.25, twice a year is 2.
If a scenario uses words like high, medium, low or a heat map, it is qualitative; if it uses currency, it is quantitative.
A control is worth buying when the reduction in ALE exceeds the annual cost of the control.
videos.realWorld: Most banks run qualitative registers for the board (a 5x5 heat map is what risk committees are used to) and reserve quantitative analysis for big decisions such as cyber insurance limits or justifying a multi-million naira SOC investment. A GRC analyst owns the KRI dashboard: each month the SOC and vulnerability teams supply the numbers, the analyst compares them to thresholds, and any breach goes to the risk owner and into the committee pack. This is also where SOC metrics like mean time to detect become risk language the board can act on.

quiz.q: A bank values its online banking platform at N500 million. A DDoS attack is expected to cause a loss of 10 percent of that value per event, and such attacks are expected twice per year. What is the ALE?
quiz.explain: SLE = N500 million x 0.10 = N50 million. ARO = 2. ALE = N50 million x 2 = N100 million. N50 million is only the SLE, and the other values do not follow from the formula.

quiz.q: A risk committee wants to compare 40 risks quickly without spending weeks gathering financial data, and several risks involve reputational harm that is hard to price. Which analysis approach is most appropriate?
options: Qualitative analysis using likelihood and impact scales
quiz.explain: Qualitative analysis is fast, needs little data and handles non-monetary harms such as reputation. Quantitative analysis requires financial data, BIA measures recovery requirements rather than ranking risks, and penetration testing is a control test.

quiz.q: A GRC analyst reports that the percentage of critical patches older than 30 days has risen from 3 percent to 9 percent, and the risk register states escalation is required above 5 percent. What have been described?
options: A key risk indicator and a risk threshold
A risk appetite and a risk owner
An exposure factor and an SLE
quiz.explain: The patch-age percentage is a measurable early-warning metric (KRI), and the 5 percent escalation level is the risk threshold. The other options describe quantitative formula components or governance concepts not present in the scenario.

videos.title: Risk Management Strategies
videos.summary: Messer covers the four risk treatment options (transfer, accept, avoid, mitigate), exemptions and exceptions, risk appetite and tolerance, and risk reporting.
videos.deepDive:
Once a risk is scored, someone has to decide what to do about it. Security+ gives four treatment strategies, and the exam tests them through scenarios where the right answer depends on cost, feasibility and the organisation's appetite.

  • Mitigate (also called reduce): implement controls that lower likelihood, impact or both. Deploying MFA, patching, segmenting the network, adding backups. This is the default and most common choice. It leaves residual risk, which must be documented and accepted.
  • Transfer (also called share): shift the financial consequence to a third party. Cyber insurance is the textbook case; outsourcing to a provider whose contract makes them liable is another. Important nuance: you can transfer financial loss but not accountability. If a processor leaks your customers' data, the regulator still fines you as the controller.
  • Avoid: stop doing the activity that creates the risk. A fintech decides not to store card numbers at all and uses tokenisation, so the risk of card data theft from its own systems disappears. Avoidance is only available when the activity is optional.
  • Accept: acknowledge the risk and take no further action because the cost of treating it exceeds the expected loss, or because it sits within appetite. Acceptance must be formal: a named risk owner signs it, with a review date. Two sub-forms are named in the objectives: an exemption is a decision that a policy or control does not apply to a system at all (a lab network isolated from production is exempt from the production patching standard); an exception is a temporary, approved deviation from a requirement that does apply, usually with a compensating control and an expiry (the legacy core banking module gets a six-month exception from the 14-character password rule while MFA is enforced in front of it).

Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk the organisation is willing to take in pursuit of its objectives, set by the board and written down. Security+ names three postures: expansionary (willing to accept higher risk for growth, typical of an early-stage fintech racing for market share), conservative (low appetite, typical of a regulated bank or a pension administrator), and neutral (balanced, accepting moderate risk where the return justifies it). Risk tolerance is the practical, measurable boundary around appetite for a specific risk: appetite says we accept low operational risk; tolerance says no more than 4 hours of unplanned payment downtime per quarter. Appetite is strategic, tolerance is operational.

Worked example: a Lagos payments company scores API abuse leading to fraudulent transfers at likelihood 4, impact 5. Options: mitigate with rate limiting, device fingerprinting and transaction monitoring (cost N30 million, reduces to 2 x 4); transfer part of the residual through a cyber insurance policy covering fraud losses up to N200 million; avoid by removing the open API (kills a revenue line, so rejected); accept the remainder. The final decision recorded in the register is mitigate and transfer, accept residual score 8 within the neutral appetite, review quarterly. Most real decisions combine strategies like this.

Risk reporting closes the loop. The GRC function reports to the risk committee and board: top risks and their trend, KRIs against thresholds, overdue treatments, new risks, accepted risks and their review dates, and exceptions expiring. The CBN framework expects cyber risk to be reported to the board at defined intervals, and ISO 27001 clause 9.3 requires management review with risk results as an input. Good reporting is short, uses consistent scales, and states what decision is being asked of the reader.

keyTerms.def: Reducing likelihood or impact by implementing controls, leaving a documented residual risk.
Shifting the financial consequence of a risk to a third party, such as through insurance or contract, without shifting accountability.
Eliminating a risk by ceasing or not starting the activity that creates it.
A formal, owner-approved decision to take no further action on a risk that sits within tolerance.
A decision that a policy or control does not apply to a particular system or situation.
A temporary, approved deviation from a requirement that does apply, usually with a compensating control and expiry date.
The amount and type of risk the organisation is willing to pursue to achieve its objectives, set by the board.
The measurable, acceptable deviation from the desired risk level for a specific risk or objective.
The risk remaining after controls have been applied.
Communicating risk status, trends, indicators and decisions to management and the board.

examTips: Insurance always equals transfer. Stopping the activity always equals avoid. Adding a control always equals mitigate. Doing nothing on purpose with sign-off equals accept.
Transferring risk never removes legal accountability; if the question asks who the regulator will fine, it is still the organisation.
Expansionary equals high appetite, conservative equals low, neutral equals balanced; match the posture to the organisation described.
Exception is temporary and needs a compensating control; exemption means the rule simply does not apply.
videos.realWorld: GRC analysts run the exception register alongside the risk register: every exception has an owner, a compensating control, an expiry date and evidence that it was approved at the right level. Expired exceptions are an easy audit finding, so the analyst chases renewals a month ahead. Cyber insurance renewals are another recurring task, because insurers now send their own questionnaires (MFA everywhere, tested backups, EDR coverage) and a weak answer raises premiums or voids cover, which turns the transfer strategy back into acceptance without anyone noticing.

quiz.q: A fintech purchases a cyber insurance policy that covers customer notification costs and regulatory fines up to a defined limit following a data breach. Which risk management strategy does this represent?
quiz.explain: Insurance shifts the financial consequence of a risk to a third party, which is transfer. It does not reduce the likelihood (mitigate), stop the activity (avoid) or knowingly retain the loss (accept).

quiz.q: A legacy loan management system cannot support the bank's MFA standard. The CISO approves a 90-day deviation, requires the system to be placed behind a jump host with MFA, and sets a date for re-review. What has been granted?
options: A risk exception with a compensating control
quiz.explain: A temporary, approved deviation from a requirement that still applies, paired with a compensating control and an expiry, is an exception. An exemption would mean the MFA standard does not apply at all. No activity was stopped or shifted to a third party.

quiz.q: A newly licensed digital lender states in its board charter that it is willing to accept elevated operational and technology risk in exchange for rapid customer growth over the next two years. Which risk appetite posture is this?
quiz.explain: Willingness to take on higher risk for growth is an expansionary appetite. Conservative would minimise risk, neutral balances it, and tolerant is not one of the named postures (tolerance is a different concept).

videos.title: Business Impact Analysis
videos.summary: Messer explains the business impact analysis and its key metrics: recovery time objective, recovery point objective, mean time to repair and mean time between failures.
videos.deepDive:
A business impact analysis (BIA) answers a different question from a risk assessment. Risk assessment asks what could go wrong and how likely is it; a BIA asks if this process stops, how bad does it get and how fast, regardless of cause. The BIA is the foundation of business continuity and disaster recovery planning, because it tells you which processes to recover first and how much data loss and downtime each can survive. ISO 22301 (business continuity) and ISO 27001 Annex A control 5.30 both expect one, and the CBN framework expects banks to maintain tested continuity and recovery arrangements.

How a BIA is done: identify business processes (not systems: interbank transfer settlement, not the switch server), interview process owners about the consequences of an outage over time (after 1 hour, 4 hours, 24 hours, 1 week), map each process to its supporting systems, people, suppliers and data, then derive the metrics below. The output ranks processes by criticality and sets recovery targets that the DR plan must meet.

The four metrics, with a worked example for a payments switch that routes instant transfers between banks:

  • Recovery time objective (RTO): the maximum acceptable time between failure and restoration of the process. If the switch is down for more than 30 minutes, transaction failures spike, customers move to competitors and the regulator notices, so RTO = 30 minutes. This forces the architecture: a 30-minute RTO cannot be met by restoring from tape; it needs an active-active or hot standby site with automatic failover.
  • Recovery point objective (RPO): the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time. For the switch, losing even a few seconds of transaction records means reconciliation nightmares and disputed transfers, so RPO = near zero, which requires synchronous replication to the standby database. Contrast with the marketing analytics warehouse, where an RPO of 24 hours (nightly backup) is fine.
  • Mean time to repair (MTTR): the average time taken to fix a failed component and return it to service, measured from historical incidents. If the switch's database cluster has failed three times in a year with repair times of 20, 40 and 30 minutes, MTTR = 30 minutes. MTTR is a measured actual; RTO is a target. If MTTR exceeds RTO you have a problem to solve before the next failure.
  • Mean time between failures (MTBF): the average operating time between one failure and the next, a reliability measure usually supplied by vendors or derived from history. If the switch's hardware security modules have run 26,000 hours with three failures, MTBF is roughly 8,700 hours, about one failure a year. MTBF feeds ARO in quantitative risk analysis and tells you how much spare capacity or redundancy to buy.

Putting them together: the BIA says the switch has RTO 30 minutes and RPO near zero. Measured MTTR is 30 minutes, which is at the limit, and MTBF suggests about one failure a year. The DR plan therefore invests in automatic failover to cut effective MTTR to under 5 minutes, and the risk register records the residual risk that a failover itself fails. Expressed in the exam's words: RTO and RPO are objectives set by the business; MTTR and MTBF are measurements of the technology, and the gap between them is what continuity planning closes.

Common confusions to settle: RPO is about data (how much can we lose), RTO is about time (how long can we be down). A system can have a short RTO and a long RPO (a public website that must be back in an hour but whose content changes weekly) or the reverse (an archive that can be down for days but must lose no records). Finally, the BIA also identifies the maximum tolerable downtime and dependencies on third parties, which is why 5.3 vendor SLAs must be checked against BIA targets: if your cloud provider offers 4-hour restoration and your RTO is 30 minutes, the contract, not the technology, is your problem.

keyTerms.def: An analysis that identifies critical business processes and quantifies the effect of their disruption over time to set recovery priorities.
The maximum acceptable time between a disruption and restoration of a process or system.
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured as the time since the last usable copy.
The average time taken to restore a failed component or system to operation, measured from actual incidents.
The average operating time between successive failures of a component, indicating reliability.
The longest outage a business process can survive before causing unacceptable harm; RTO must be shorter than MTD.
A fully equipped, continuously synchronised alternate site that supports very short RTO and RPO.

examTips: RPO is about data loss and drives backup or replication frequency; RTO is about downtime and drives recovery architecture.
MTTR and MTBF are measurements from history or vendor data; RTO and RPO are business targets. If MTTR exceeds RTO, the recovery capability is inadequate.
A near-zero RPO in a scenario points to synchronous replication or a hot site; a 24-hour RPO points to daily backups.
BIA comes before DR planning; if a question asks what to do first when building continuity plans, the answer is the BIA.
videos.realWorld: In a bank the GRC or business continuity team runs the BIA annually with every department head, and the results become the tiering used everywhere else: Tier 1 processes (payments, core banking, ATM switching) get RTOs measured in minutes and are tested in the annual DR exercise that the CBN expects evidence of; Tier 3 processes get days. SOC analysts meet the same numbers during incidents, where the incident severity rating is often defined by which BIA tier is affected, and MTTR for security incidents is a reported KRI.

quiz.q: A payments switch operator determines that losing more than 5 seconds of transaction data would cause irreconcilable disputes between banks. Which BIA metric has been set, and what does it imply for the design?
options: RPO of 5 seconds, requiring synchronous or near-synchronous replication
MTBF of 5 seconds, requiring more reliable hardware
MTTR of 5 seconds, requiring automated ticketing
RTO of 5 seconds, requiring faster staff response
quiz.explain: Acceptable data loss expressed as time is the RPO. Meeting a 5-second RPO requires replication that keeps the standby copy almost continuously current. RTO is downtime, MTBF is reliability and MTTR is repair time.

quiz.q: A bank's BIA sets an RTO of 1 hour for its mobile banking service. Incident records show the last four outages took 2, 3, 1.5 and 2.5 hours to resolve. What conclusion should the continuity team draw?
options: The RPO is too aggressive and should be relaxed
The MTTR of about 2.25 hours exceeds the RTO, so recovery capability must be improved
The MTBF is too low and hardware should be replaced
The service is meeting its recovery objective
quiz.explain: Average repair time is (2 + 3 + 1.5 + 2.5) / 4 = 2.25 hours, which exceeds the 1-hour RTO. The scenario gives no data-loss or failure-frequency information, so RPO and MTBF conclusions are unsupported.

quiz.q: A fintech is starting to build its first disaster recovery plan. Which activity should it complete first to determine which systems to prioritise?
options: Sign an SLA with a cloud provider
quiz.explain: The BIA identifies critical processes and their recovery requirements, which determine what the DR plan must protect and how. Buying a site or signing an SLA before knowing the requirements risks wasted spend, and a penetration test addresses vulnerabilities, not recovery priorities.

objectives.title: Explain the processes associated with third-party risk assessment and management

videos.title: Third-party Risk Assessment
videos.summary: Messer explains how to assess vendors before and during a relationship: penetration testing, right-to-audit clauses, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments, supply chain analysis, due diligence, conflicts of interest, questionnaires, rules of engagement and ongoing monitoring.
videos.deepDive:
Every organisation now runs on other people's systems: cloud hosting, payment processors, SMS gateways, core banking vendors, KYC providers, outsourced call centres. Each one is a door into your environment and your data, and attackers know it: the most damaging breaches of the last decade (Target through an HVAC contractor, SolarWinds through a software update, MOVEit through a file transfer product) came through third parties. Third-party risk management (TPRM) is the discipline of deciding which vendors to trust, verifying that trust before signing, and re-verifying it for as long as the relationship lasts. The CBN framework and the NDPA both make you responsible for what your vendors do with your systems and data, so outsourcing the work never outsources the accountability.

Vendor selection starts with due diligence: investigating the vendor before commitment. Financial stability (will they exist in three years), ownership and beneficial owners, litigation and regulatory history, certifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, PCI DSS attestation of compliance), breach history, key staff, sub-contractors and where data will physically reside. A conflict of interest check ensures the people choosing the vendor have no undisclosed stake in it: a procurement head whose brother owns the shortlisted firm must recuse. Both are also anti-fraud controls, which is why procurement and security run them together.

Vendor assessment techniques the objectives list:

  • Questionnaires: structured self-assessments the vendor completes, often based on standard sets such as the SIG (Standardised Information Gathering) or CAIQ for cloud providers. Cheap and scalable, but self-reported, so answers must be backed by evidence for high-risk vendors.
  • Evidence of internal audits: the vendor's own audit reports and remediation tracking show whether they check themselves and fix what they find.
  • Independent assessments: third-party reports such as a SOC 2 Type II (controls tested over a period by an external auditor), an ISO 27001 certificate with its statement of applicability, or a PCI DSS report on compliance. These are stronger than questionnaires because someone outside the vendor verified them.
  • Penetration testing: either the vendor's own recent test report with remediation status, or, for critical integrations, a test you commission against the interface they expose to you. This requires agreed rules of engagement: a written agreement defining scope (which IP ranges, applications and accounts), timing, permitted techniques, exclusions, emergency contacts and how findings are handled, so your testers do not accidentally attack shared infrastructure serving other clients.
  • Right-to-audit clause: a contract term giving you the right to inspect the vendor's controls, premises and records, yourself or through a nominated auditor, with notice. Without this clause you have no leverage when a questionnaire answer looks wrong. Regulators expect banks to hold this right over material outsourcing partners.
  • Supply chain analysis: looking beyond the direct vendor to their vendors. Your cloud SMS provider uses an upstream aggregator, which uses telco APIs; your core banking vendor embeds open-source libraries. Mapping the fourth parties and the software bill of materials tells you where concentration risk hides: if six of your critical vendors all run on the same hosting provider, one outage takes all six down.

Vendor monitoring is the ongoing part. Vendors are tiered by criticality (a payments processor is Tier 1, the office plant supplier is Tier 4) and the tier sets the cadence: annual reassessment and evidence refresh for Tier 1, questionnaire every two years for Tier 3. Between reviews, monitoring includes SLA performance reports, security rating services that scan the vendor's external footprint, breach notifications, news, certificate expiry tracking and a review whenever the vendor's scope or ownership changes.

Worked example: a bank onboarding a fintech for bill payments. Due diligence: CAC records, CBN licence check, audited financials, beneficial owner screening against sanctions lists. Assessment: SIG questionnaire, SOC 2 Type II report, last penetration test summary, data flow diagram showing where customer data goes. Contract: right-to-audit, breach notification within 24 hours, sub-processor approval, exit and data return terms. Monitoring: quarterly SLA review, annual reassessment, continuous external rating. The GRC analyst owns this file for the life of the contract.

keyTerms.def: The process of identifying, assessing and monitoring the risks introduced by vendors, suppliers and partners.
Investigating a vendor's financial, legal, operational and security standing before entering a relationship.
A situation where a decision maker's personal interests could improperly influence a vendor selection.
A contract term giving the customer the right to inspect a vendor's controls, records and facilities.
An evaluation of a vendor's controls performed by an external party, such as a SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certification audit.
Examining a vendor's own suppliers, sub-processors and components to find hidden or concentrated risk.
A written agreement defining scope, timing, methods, contacts and limits for a penetration test.
A structured self-assessment a vendor completes about its security practices, often based on a standard such as SIG.
Ongoing review of a vendor's performance, security posture and compliance throughout the relationship.

examTips: If a scenario says the vendor refuses to let you verify their claims, the missing item is a right-to-audit clause.
Questionnaires are self-reported; when the question asks for stronger assurance, choose an independent assessment such as a SOC 2 Type II report.
Rules of engagement are agreed before any penetration test, including one against a vendor; testing without them is unauthorised.
Supply chain analysis looks at the vendor's vendors; if the scenario mentions a component or sub-contractor, that is the clue.
videos.realWorld: Bank GRC teams run a vendor inventory with tiers, and the annual reassessment cycle for Tier 1 vendors is a full-time workload in itself: chasing renewed SOC 2 reports, reading the exceptions section rather than just the cover page, checking the ISO certificate scope actually covers the service you buy, and escalating vendors whose external security rating drops. Regulators increasingly ask to see the material outsourcing register and evidence that right-to-audit has actually been exercised at least once, not just written into contracts.

quiz.q: A bank is selecting a cloud provider to host customer data. The provider's questionnaire answers are all positive, but the bank's GRC team wants assurance that the controls were tested by someone outside the vendor over a period of time. Which evidence best meets this need?
options: A verbal assurance from the vendor's CEO
A SOC 2 Type II report from an independent auditor
quiz.explain: A SOC 2 Type II report is an independent assessment in which an external auditor tests control operation over a period. Questionnaires and whitepapers are self-reported, and verbal assurances carry no evidentiary weight.

quiz.q: Two years into a contract, a payment processor suffers a breach and declines to share details of its investigation or allow the bank to inspect its controls. Which contract provision would have prevented this situation?
options: A service level agreement for uptime
quiz.explain: A right-to-audit clause gives the customer the contractual right to inspect the vendor's controls and records. An NDA restricts disclosure, an MOU is non-binding, and an uptime SLA does not grant inspection rights.

quiz.q: A fintech discovers that five of its critical vendors, including its SMS gateway and KYC provider, all depend on the same upstream hosting company. Which assessment activity revealed this concentration risk?
quiz.explain: Supply chain analysis examines the vendors' own suppliers and dependencies, which is how shared upstream reliance is discovered. Conflict of interest concerns decision makers, penetration testing finds technical vulnerabilities, and financial due diligence assesses solvency.

videos.title: Agreement Types
videos.summary: Messer walks through the main third-party agreements: SLA, MOA, MOU, MSA, WO/SOW, NDA and BPA, and what each is used for.
videos.deepDive:
Contracts are the control that makes every other vendor control enforceable. Security+ tests seven agreement types, and the questions are almost always which document would contain this, so learn what each one actually holds.

  • Service level agreement (SLA): defines measurable service targets and the remedies if they are missed. Contents: availability (99.95 percent monthly uptime), performance (API response under 300 ms at the 95th percentile), support response and resolution times by severity (Severity 1 acknowledged in 15 minutes, resolved in 4 hours), security obligations (breach notification within 24 hours, patching of critical vulnerabilities within 14 days), reporting cadence, and service credits or termination rights on breach. The SLA is where BIA targets meet the vendor: your RTO must fit inside the vendor's committed restoration time.
  • Memorandum of understanding (MOU): a written statement of intent between parties who plan to work together, describing roles and expectations in general terms. Usually not legally binding. Used for early-stage partnerships, inter-agency cooperation, or two banks agreeing to share threat intelligence before formal terms exist.
  • Memorandum of agreement (MOA): more formal than an MOU, with specific commitments and often conditional obligations, and it may be binding depending on wording. The exam treats MOU and MOA as similar, with MOA being the more detailed and committed of the two. Both are lighter than a full contract.
  • Master service agreement (MSA): the overarching contract that sets the general legal terms for a long relationship: payment terms, liability caps, indemnities, intellectual property, confidentiality, governing law, dispute resolution, termination, data protection and audit rights. It is negotiated once so that individual pieces of work do not need to renegotiate the legal basics.
  • Work order (WO) or statement of work (SOW): the document under an MSA that defines one specific engagement: deliverables, scope, milestones, acceptance criteria, timeline, named resources and price. A penetration testing SOW, for example, lists the target systems, test dates, methodology, reporting format and the number of retest days. Many SOWs can hang off one MSA.
  • Non-disclosure agreement (NDA): protects confidential information exchanged between parties. Defines what counts as confidential, permitted uses, who may see it, how long the obligation lasts and what happens on termination. Can be one-way (you show a vendor your architecture) or mutual. Signed before due diligence starts, because the assessment itself exposes sensitive details on both sides.
  • Business partnership agreement (BPA): governs a partnership where the parties share in a business venture: how profits and losses are split, each party's contributions and responsibilities, decision rights, and exit terms. A bank and a fintech co-launching a product, with shared revenue, would use a BPA rather than a simple supplier contract.

Worked example, in order: a bank and a Lagos identity-verification startup want to work together. They sign an NDA so both sides can share technical detail. They sign an MOU to record the intended scope of a pilot. Legal negotiates an MSA covering liability, data protection under the NDPA, right-to-audit and termination. The first SOW defines the pilot integration: deliverables, dates, acceptance tests, N12 million fee. An SLA schedule commits to 99.9 percent API uptime and 24-hour breach notification. Later, when they agree to co-brand the product and share revenue, they sign a BPA. Each document answers a different question, and the exam gives you one of those questions.

What a GRC analyst checks in these documents: that the SLA metrics are measurable and actually reported, that breach notification timelines are short enough to let the bank meet its own NDPC and CBN obligations, that the MSA contains right-to-audit and sub-processor approval clauses, that the SOW for any security testing includes rules of engagement, and that the NDA is in place before any data is exchanged. Weak contract terms are a risk register entry like any other.

keyTerms.def: A contract defining measurable service targets such as uptime and response time, with remedies if they are missed.
A generally non-binding written statement of intent describing how parties plan to work together.
A more formal and specific agreement of commitments between parties, potentially binding, but lighter than a full contract.
An overarching contract setting general legal terms for a relationship, under which individual work orders are issued.
A document defining the scope, deliverables, timeline, acceptance criteria and price of one specific engagement.
