A contract protecting confidential information shared between parties, either one-way or mutual.
A contract defining responsibilities, contributions, profit sharing and exit terms between business partners in a joint venture.
A financial remedy the vendor owes when an SLA target is missed.

examTips: Uptime percentages and response times equal SLA. Profit sharing equals BPA. Confidentiality equals NDA. Specific deliverables and price equal SOW. General legal terms for a long relationship equal MSA. Non-binding intent equals MOU.
The MSA is signed once; SOWs are signed per project underneath it. If a question describes a repeated engagement under existing terms, the new document is a SOW.
The NDA comes first chronologically, before any sensitive information is exchanged during due diligence.
videos.realWorld: GRC analysts in banks are routinely asked by Legal and Procurement to review the security schedule of vendor contracts before signature. The practical checklist is short: breach notification within 24 hours so the bank can meet its 72-hour NDPC deadline, right-to-audit, data location and return on exit, sub-processor approval, and SLA metrics that match the BIA tier of the service. When a vendor misses an SLA, the analyst is the one who pulls the monthly report and calculates the service credit owed.

quiz.q: A bank wants its cloud provider to commit contractually to 99.95 percent monthly availability, a 4-hour resolution time for critical incidents, and service credits if these are missed. Which agreement type should contain these terms?
quiz.explain: Measurable service targets and remedies for missing them are the content of an SLA. An MOU is non-binding intent, an NDA covers confidentiality, and a BPA covers partnership profit sharing and responsibilities.

quiz.q: A bank already has a master service agreement with a security consultancy. It now wants the consultancy to perform a specific web application penetration test with defined targets, dates, deliverables and a fixed fee. Which document should be created?
quiz.explain: A specific engagement with defined scope, deliverables, timeline and price under an existing MSA is documented in a statement of work. The MSA already exists and does not need replacing, and an MOA or BPA is the wrong instrument.

quiz.q: Before allowing a prospective vendor to review its network architecture during due diligence, a fintech wants legal protection against the vendor disclosing or misusing that information. Which agreement is needed first?
quiz.explain: An NDA protects confidential information exchanged between parties and is signed before sensitive details are shared. The SLA, SOW and MSA govern service delivery and general terms, not the confidentiality of pre-contract disclosures.

objectives.title: Summarize elements of effective security compliance

videos.title: Compliance
videos.summary: Messer covers compliance reporting (internal and external), the consequences of non-compliance, and compliance monitoring through due diligence, due care, attestation, acknowledgement and automation.
videos.deepDive:
Compliance means meeting the requirements imposed on you by law, regulators, industry standards and your own policies, and being able to prove it. Security and compliance are not the same thing: you can be compliant and insecure (all boxes ticked, still breached) or secure and non-compliant (strong controls, no evidence), and the exam expects you to see compliance as the proof layer sitting on top of the control layer. In a bank, compliance is what keeps the licence; in a fintech, it is what keeps the bank partnership.

Compliance reporting comes in two directions. Internal reporting goes to management, the audit committee and the board: dashboards of control status, open findings and their age, policy attestation completion, KRI trends, exceptions outstanding. Its purpose is to let leadership steer and to demonstrate oversight. External reporting goes to regulators, auditors, customers and partners: the annual return to the CBN under the cybersecurity framework, incident reports within the regulator's deadline, the NDPA compliance audit filing to the Nigeria Data Protection Commission for data controllers of major importance, PCI DSS attestations to the acquiring bank, SWIFT CSP attestations, and SOC 2 reports for enterprise customers. External reports carry legal weight, so they are reviewed by Legal and signed by an accountable executive.

Consequences of non-compliance, all of which appear on the exam:

  • Fines: monetary penalties. The NDPA allows the NDPC to impose penalties on data controllers of major importance of up to the greater of N10 million or 2 percent of annual gross revenue for the preceding year. The CBN routinely fines banks for breaches of its circulars.
  • Sanctions: non-monetary regulatory action such as restrictions on new products, suspension from certain activities, mandated remediation programmes, or public censure.
  • Reputational damage: customer churn, negative press and loss of partner confidence, often costlier than the fine.
  • Loss of licence: the ultimate sanction. A CBN-licensed payment provider that cannot demonstrate compliance can have its licence suspended or revoked, ending the business.
  • Contractual impacts: a bank partner terminates the agreement, PCI non-compliance leads the acquirer to raise fees or stop card processing, and SLA breaches trigger penalties.

Compliance monitoring is how you know you are compliant before someone else finds out you are not. Its components:

  • Due diligence is investigating before acting (researching the rules that apply, assessing a vendor); due care is then acting as a reasonable, prudent organisation would (implementing the controls, maintaining them). Courts and regulators ask whether you exercised both. A memorable pairing: due diligence is doing your homework, due care is doing the work.
  • Attestation: a formal statement by a responsible person or independent party that a control or requirement is met. A control owner attests quarterly that the access review was completed; an executive attests to the regulator that the framework is implemented.
  • Acknowledgement: a user's confirmation that they have received and understood a policy, such as signing the AUP or completing the annual policy read-through. Acknowledgement records are what you produce when someone claims they did not know the rule.
  • Internal monitoring (compliance team reviews, control self-assessments, internal audit) versus external monitoring (regulator examinations, external audits, customer assessments).
  • Automation: GRC platforms and compliance tooling that pull evidence from systems directly: an API check that MFA is enforced on every admin account, a nightly scan that confirms encryption settings, automated collection of access review completions. Automation turns point-in-time compliance into continuous compliance and cuts the audit preparation scramble.

Worked example: a fintech maps CBN framework clause multi-factor authentication for privileged access to control AC-07 in its GRC tool. The tool queries the identity provider daily and reports coverage. The IT head attests quarterly that exceptions are documented. The compliance officer includes the coverage trend in the internal dashboard and the annual CBN return. If coverage drops below the 100 percent threshold, a ticket opens automatically. That is compliance monitoring end to end, and it is the workflow a GRC analyst builds and runs.

keyTerms.def: Meeting and demonstrating adherence to legal, regulatory, contractual and internal policy requirements.
Reporting control and compliance status to management, audit committees and the board to support oversight.
Reporting compliance status to regulators, auditors, customers or partners, often with legal consequences.
Investigating and understanding obligations and risks before taking action.
Taking the reasonable, prudent actions that a responsible organisation would take to meet obligations and protect assets.
A formal declaration by a responsible person or independent party that a requirement or control is satisfied.
A user's recorded confirmation that they have received and understood a policy or requirement.
A non-monetary regulatory penalty such as activity restrictions, mandated remediation or public censure.
Using tooling to collect evidence and test controls continuously rather than through manual point-in-time checks.

examTips: Due diligence is research before action; due care is the action itself. If the scenario describes investigating, it is diligence; if it describes implementing or maintaining, it is care.
Attestation is made by the responsible party or an auditor about a control; acknowledgement is made by a user about a policy.
Loss of licence is the most severe consequence and is tied to regulators; contractual impacts come from partners and customers.
If a question asks how to reduce the effort of proving compliance repeatedly, the answer involves automation.
videos.realWorld: A compliance or GRC analyst at a Nigerian fintech keeps an obligations calendar: CBN returns, NDPC annual audit filings, PCI DSS attestation renewals, SWIFT CSP attestation, ISO surveillance audits. Each has evidence owners and due dates, and missing one is a career-limiting event. Increasingly the analyst also administers the GRC platform, wiring integrations so that evidence such as MFA coverage or backup success rates is collected automatically, and the quarterly attestation campaign to control owners runs from the same tool.

quiz.q: A fintech's compliance officer researches which CBN circulars and NDPA provisions apply to a new savings product before launch, and then the engineering team implements the required controls and maintains them. Which two concepts are illustrated, in order?
quiz.explain: Researching the applicable obligations before acting is due diligence; implementing and maintaining the controls is due care. The other pairs describe reporting or consequences, not this sequence.

quiz.q: A payment service provider repeatedly fails to submit required cybersecurity returns to its regulator and cannot demonstrate a functioning security programme. Which consequence of non-compliance is the most severe outcome it faces?
quiz.explain: Regulators can suspend or revoke the licence of a supervised entity that fails to comply, which ends the business. The other options are minor or internal consequences.

quiz.q: An organisation spends three weeks before each audit manually collecting screenshots proving that MFA is enabled on administrator accounts. Which improvement to compliance monitoring would most reduce this effort while increasing assurance?
options: Move the audit to every two years
Ask the auditor to accept a verbal attestation
Require administrators to sign a yearly acknowledgement
Automate evidence collection by querying the identity provider continuously
quiz.explain: Compliance automation collects evidence directly and continuously, cutting manual effort and giving stronger, current assurance. Acknowledgements and verbal statements are weaker evidence, and reducing audit frequency reduces assurance.

videos.title: Privacy
videos.summary: Messer covers privacy obligations across local, regional, national and global law, the data subject, controller versus processor, data ownership, data inventory and retention, and the right to be forgotten.
videos.deepDive:
Privacy is the set of rights individuals hold over information about themselves, and privacy law turns those rights into obligations for the organisations that hold the data. Security protects data from unauthorised access; privacy limits what even authorised parties may do with it. A bank can have perfect encryption and still violate privacy by using account data for marketing without a lawful basis. Security+ tests the legal structure of privacy at a high level, and for a Nigerian learner the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 is the concrete example that makes the abstract terms real.

Legal implications by geography. Local rules are rare for privacy but exist for things like CCTV in specific premises. Regional frameworks include the African Union's Malabo Convention on cyber security and personal data protection and ECOWAS's supplementary act on personal data, which shape national laws across West Africa. National law is the main event: in Nigeria the NDPA 2023, which established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) and sits alongside the earlier NDPR 2019; in the EU the GDPR; in the US a patchwork of sector laws (HIPAA for health, GLBA for finance) and state laws such as the CCPA. Global implications arise because laws such as the GDPR and the NDPA apply to organisations outside their borders when they target or process the data of residents, and because cross-border transfers require an adequacy decision, contractual safeguards or another lawful mechanism. A Lagos fintech with EU customers is bound by both laws, and a Nigerian bank moving data to a foreign cloud must satisfy the NDPA's transfer rules.

Roles, now from the privacy side. The data subject is the living individual the data is about, and they hold the rights: to be informed, to access their data, to rectify errors, to erase (the right to be forgotten), to restrict or object to processing, and to data portability. The controller determines why and how personal data is processed and answers for these rights; the processor acts on the controller's instructions. The NDPA also requires controllers and processors of major importance to register with the NDPC, appoint a Data Protection Officer, conduct data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, and notify the NDPC of a breach likely to risk individuals' rights within 72 hours, and affected data subjects without undue delay.

Ownership is a subtle point. Legally, personal data is not owned like property; the data subject has rights over it and the controller has responsibilities for it. Inside the organisation, however, a data owner (from 5.1) is still assigned for accountability. The exam may ask who owns customer data, and the safe framing is that the organisation is accountable as controller while the individual retains rights.

Data inventory and retention. You cannot honour rights over data you cannot find, so controllers maintain a data inventory (a record of processing activities): what personal data is held, why, on what lawful basis, where it is stored, who it is shared with, which processors touch it and how long it is kept. Retention must be limited to what the purpose requires or the law mandates: Nigerian anti-money-laundering rules require banks to keep customer identification records for at least five years after the relationship ends, so a bank cannot erase KYC records on request even under the right to be forgotten, and that legal obligation is a valid ground to refuse. Beyond the mandated period, data must be deleted or anonymised on schedule.

Right to be forgotten in practice: a former customer of a Lagos lending app requests erasure. The DPO checks the inventory, finds the data in the loan platform, the CRM, a marketing tool and a processor's SMS logs. Marketing and CRM data are erased and the processor is instructed to erase its copy. Loan and KYC records are retained under the AML obligation, and the customer is told why, in writing, within the statutory response time. Every step is logged, because the NDPC can ask for the audit trail. That workflow is what a privacy or GRC analyst runs, and the data inventory is the tool that makes it possible.

keyTerms.def: The right of individuals to control how information about them is collected, used, shared and retained.
Nigeria's principal data protection law, establishing the NDPC and defining controller, processor and data subject obligations and rights.
The identifiable living person to whom personal data relates and who holds privacy rights over it.
The data subject's right to have personal data erased when there is no longer a lawful reason to retain it.
A record of what personal data an organisation holds, why, where, with whom it is shared and for how long.
Keeping data only as long as the purpose or law requires, then deleting or anonymising it.
Moving personal data to another country, permitted only under an adequacy decision, contractual safeguards or another lawful mechanism.
A documented assessment of privacy risks required before high-risk processing of personal data.
The legal duty to inform the regulator, and often data subjects, of a personal data breach within a set time such as 72 hours.

examTips: Controller decides, processor follows instructions, data subject holds the rights; every privacy question maps to one of these three.
The right to be forgotten is not absolute; a legal retention obligation such as anti-money-laundering record keeping is a valid reason to refuse erasure.
A data inventory is the prerequisite for honouring data subject rights and for setting retention; if a scenario says the organisation does not know where its personal data is, that is the answer.
Global privacy questions usually hinge on extraterritorial reach or cross-border transfer restrictions.
videos.realWorld: In Nigerian banks and larger fintechs the DPO sits with GRC or Legal, and a GRC analyst often runs the operational side: maintaining the record of processing activities, logging and tracking data subject requests to the statutory deadline, coordinating DPIAs for new products, preparing the annual NDPC compliance audit filing, and running the breach notification playbook alongside the SOC when an incident involves personal data. SOC analysts feed this by flagging, during triage, whether an incident touched personal data, because that single fact starts the 72-hour clock.

quiz.q: A former customer of a Nigerian digital bank requests that all their personal data be erased. The bank deletes marketing and CRM records but retains the customer's identity documents and transaction history. Which is the best justification for the partial refusal?
options: A legal retention obligation under anti-money-laundering rules overrides the erasure request for those records
The right to be forgotten only applies to EU residents
Processors are not required to honour data subject rights
The bank owns the data and can keep it indefinitely
quiz.explain: The right to be forgotten is not absolute; a statutory obligation to retain records is a lawful ground to refuse erasure of those specific records while still erasing everything else. Organisations do not own personal data outright, the NDPA grants the right to Nigerian data subjects, and the bank here is the controller.

quiz.q: A fintech is preparing to handle data subject access requests but discovers it does not know which systems and vendors hold customer personal data. What should it create first?
options: A data inventory or record of processing activities
quiz.explain: A data inventory documents what personal data is held, where, why and with which processors, and is the prerequisite for locating data to honour any request. The other options do not solve the discovery problem.

quiz.q: A Lagos-based remittance company serves customers living in Germany and stores their data on servers in Nigeria. Which privacy consideration most directly affects it?
options: None, because the servers are in Nigeria
Global implications, because the GDPR applies to it as a non-EU organisation serving EU residents and governs transfers of their data
quiz.explain: The GDPR has extraterritorial reach and applies to organisations outside the EU that offer services to EU residents, and transfers of their data to Nigeria require a lawful transfer mechanism. Server location alone does not exempt the company.

objectives.title: Explain types and purposes of audits and assessments

videos.title: Audits and Assessments
videos.summary: Messer explains attestation, internal audits and assessments (compliance, audit committee, self-assessments) and external ones (regulatory examinations, assessments, independent third-party audits).
videos.deepDive:
An audit answers one question: do the controls you say you have actually exist and work? It is the difference between believing you are secure and being able to prove it to someone who does not take your word for it. Security+ splits audits and assessments into internal and external, and adds attestation as the formal output. The distinctions matter because the exam asks which kind of review a scenario describes and who performs it.

First, the vocabulary. An assessment is a broad evaluation of security posture against a framework or set of objectives, often advisory, that produces findings and recommendations. An audit is a formal, evidence-based examination against defined criteria that produces a pass or fail conclusion on each control, usually with a documented opinion. Assessments tell you where you stand; audits tell a third party whether they can rely on you. Attestation is the formal declaration that results: management attests that controls are in place, or an auditor attests that they tested them and gives an opinion. A SOC 2 report is an attestation engagement; a signed CBN cybersecurity return is a management attestation.

Internal audits and assessments are performed by the organisation's own people, ideally independent of the function being reviewed.

  • Compliance reviews check adherence to internal policy and external obligations: has every policy been reviewed on schedule, have all staff completed awareness training, are exceptions current.
  • Audit committee: a committee of the board (in Nigerian banks typically including independent non-executive directors, as required by CBN corporate governance guidelines) that oversees internal audit, receives its reports, tracks remediation of findings and appoints the external auditor. Internal audit reports to the audit committee, not to the CISO or CIO, precisely so that it can criticise them.
  • Self-assessments: control owners evaluate their own controls against a checklist, such as a control self-assessment questionnaire or the NIST CSF 2.0 tiers, or a PCI DSS self-assessment questionnaire for smaller merchants. Cheap and educational, but weak assurance because the person marking the paper wrote it, which is why self-assessments feed audits rather than replace them.

External audits and assessments are performed by parties outside the organisation.

  • Regulatory: reviews required by a supervisor. In Nigeria the CBN framework requires banks to conduct periodic independent assessments of their cybersecurity programme and report to the regulator.
  • Examinations: the regulator itself comes in. CBN examiners perform on-site and off-site examinations of banks, review the risk register, interview the CISO, sample controls and issue findings with deadlines. The NDPC can also investigate data controllers. Examinations are the most consequential kind of external review because the examiner can impose sanctions directly.
  • Assessment: an external consultancy evaluates posture against a framework (an ISO 27001 gap assessment, a NIST CSF maturity assessment) and gives recommendations, without issuing a formal opinion.
  • Independent third-party audit: an accredited external auditor tests controls against a standard and issues a formal opinion or certificate: ISO 27001 certification by an accredited certification body, a SOC 2 Type II report by a licensed CPA firm, a PCI DSS report on compliance by a Qualified Security Assessor. These are what customers and partners rely on, and independence is the whole point: the auditor must have no stake in the outcome.

Worked example of an audit cycle at a Nigerian bank: Q1, control owners complete self-assessments in the GRC tool. Q2, internal audit tests a sample of high-risk controls, finds that 12 percent of leaver accounts were disabled late, and reports to the audit committee with a remediation date. Q3, the ISO 27001 certification body performs its surveillance audit, reviews the internal audit results and remediation evidence, and issues a minor non-conformity if the fix is incomplete. Q4, CBN examiners review the same evidence during their examination. One set of evidence, four reviewers with increasing independence and consequence. The GRC analyst's job across all four is the same: know where the evidence is, make sure it is current, and track every finding to closure.

keyTerms.def: A formal, evidence-based examination of controls against defined criteria that produces a documented conclusion or opinion.
An evaluation of security posture against a framework or objectives that produces findings and recommendations, often advisory.
A formal declaration by management or an independent auditor that controls or requirements are met.
A board committee that oversees internal and external audit, receives findings and tracks remediation, independent of management.
An evaluation of controls performed by the control owners themselves, providing low-cost but weak assurance.
A review performed directly by a regulator, such as the CBN, that can result in binding findings and sanctions.
An audit by an accredited external party with no stake in the outcome, producing a certificate or formal report such as ISO 27001 or SOC 2.
An audit finding that a requirement of the standard is not met, classified as major or minor in ISO audits.

examTips: Internal audit reports to the audit committee of the board, not to IT or security management; questions about independence of internal audit test this.
Self-assessment gives the weakest assurance and independent third-party audit the strongest; choose according to how much assurance the scenario demands.
An examination is performed by the regulator itself; an external audit is performed by an accredited private firm; do not swap them.
Attestation is the output of an audit or a management declaration, not a type of test.
videos.realWorld: GRC analysts spend a large share of the year in audit support: preparing evidence request lists, walking auditors through controls, and managing the findings tracker. The skill that separates a good analyst is mapping once and reusing everywhere: the same access review evidence satisfies ISO 27001 Annex A, the CBN examiner and the SOC 2 auditor, if it is stored and labelled properly. SOC analysts meet audits when asked to demonstrate that alerts fire, that logs are retained for the required period, and that incident tickets show the response timeline.

quiz.q: A bank's internal audit team finds that privileged access reviews were skipped for two quarters. To preserve independence, to whom should internal audit report this finding?
options: The vendor that supplies the identity system
The CISO, who owns the control
The audit committee of the board
quiz.explain: Internal audit reports to the board's audit committee so that it remains independent of the management functions it reviews. Reporting only to the CISO or IT would compromise that independence, and the vendor is not part of governance.

quiz.q: An enterprise customer will only sign with a fintech if the fintech can demonstrate that its security controls were tested by an accredited external party over a period of time. Which type of review satisfies this?
options: An independent third-party audit such as a SOC 2 Type II
A regulatory examination by the CBN
quiz.explain: An independent third-party audit by an accredited firm produces a formal report customers can rely on. Self-assessments and internal reviews lack independence, and a regulatory examination is performed by the regulator for its own purposes, not for customers.

quiz.q: Examiners from the central bank arrive on-site, review the bank's cyber risk register, interview the CISO, sample controls and issue findings with mandatory deadlines. Which type of review is this?
quiz.explain: A review conducted directly by the regulator with binding findings is a regulatory examination. Third-party audits are done by accredited private firms, self-assessments by control owners, and vendor assessments evaluate suppliers.

videos.title: Penetration Tests
videos.summary: Messer covers penetration test types (physical, offensive, defensive, integrated), known, partially known and unknown environments, and passive versus active reconnaissance.
videos.deepDive:
A penetration test is an authorised, simulated attack against your systems, people or premises to find out what a real attacker could achieve. A vulnerability scan lists weaknesses; a penetration test proves which of them can actually be exploited and chained together to reach something valuable. That difference (exploitation and impact demonstration versus enumeration) is the first contrast the exam tests. Penetration testing is required by PCI DSS at least annually and after significant change, and the CBN framework expects Nigerian banks to conduct penetration tests regularly, so it is a compliance obligation as well as a security practice.

Every test starts with rules of engagement (from 5.3): scope, dates, allowed techniques, exclusions such as production databases during business hours, emergency stop contacts, and evidence handling. Testing without written authorisation is a crime under the Nigerian Cybercrimes Act and everywhere else, so the authorisation letter is the tester's most important document.

Types by target and posture:

  • Physical: testers attempt to enter premises, tailgate through doors, clone badges, plant rogue devices or access unattended workstations. Tests whether the physical security standard holds in practice.
  • Offensive: the red team acts as the attacker, attempting to breach defences and reach agreed objectives such as accessing the payment switch or exfiltrating a test file.
  • Defensive: the blue team, usually the SOC, focuses on detecting and responding to the attack. A defensive test measures detection coverage, alert quality and response time rather than just whether the attacker got in.
  • Integrated: offensive and defensive teams work together, often called purple teaming. The red team runs a technique, the blue team checks whether it was detected, and detections are tuned on the spot. Integrated testing gives the most improvement per day of effort, which is why mature SOCs prefer it.

Types by knowledge given to the tester:

  • Known environment (historically white box): testers receive full information: architecture diagrams, source code, credentials, configurations. Most thorough for the time spent because no effort goes into discovery; best for deep application or code review.
  • Unknown environment (black box): testers receive nothing but the company name or a target range. Most realistic simulation of an external attacker, but slow and may miss issues that discovery does not reach.
  • Partially known environment (grey box): testers receive some information, such as a standard user account and the application URL. Simulates an insider or a customer who has turned malicious, and is the most common choice for web and mobile application tests because it balances realism and coverage.

Reconnaissance is the discovery phase. Passive reconnaissance gathers information without touching the target's systems: WHOIS and DNS records, certificate transparency logs, job adverts revealing technologies, LinkedIn for staff names and email formats, leaked credential databases, Shodan results, public code repositories. It is undetectable by the target. Active reconnaissance interacts with the target: port scanning with nmap, banner grabbing, web crawling, vulnerability scanning, DNS zone transfer attempts. It is detectable and shows up in the SOC's logs, which is exactly why defensive tests use it to measure whether the SOC notices.

Worked example: a Lagos fintech commissions a partially known environment test of its mobile banking API. Rules of engagement limit testing to the staging environment mirrored from production, weekday hours, with two test customer accounts. Passive reconnaissance finds an old subdomain in certificate logs and a developer's public repository containing an API key. Active reconnaissance enumerates endpoints. The testers chain the leaked key with a broken object-level authorisation flaw to read another test customer's transactions. The report rates this critical, the SOC review shows the enumeration generated no alerts, and the integrated follow-up tunes a rate-limit detection. Three findings from one test: a vulnerability, a secrets-management failure, and a detection gap.

keyTerms.def: An authorised simulated attack that attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to demonstrate real-world impact.
A test where the testers are given full information such as architecture, code and credentials.
A test where the testers are given no internal information, simulating an external attacker.
A test where the testers receive limited information, such as a user account, simulating an insider or customer.
Red team activity that attempts to breach defences and reach defined objectives.
Blue team activity that measures the ability to detect and respond to attacks.
Red and blue teams working together, often called purple teaming, to test and improve detection in real time.
Gathering information about a target from public sources without directly interacting with its systems.
Gathering information by directly interacting with the target, such as port scanning, which can be detected.
An authorised attempt to bypass physical security controls such as doors, badges and guards.

examTips: If the testers touch the target (scanning, probing, connecting), it is active reconnaissance; if they only read public sources, it is passive.
Full information equals known environment, none equals unknown, some equals partially known; the older white, black and grey box terms may still appear.
Red and blue working together equals integrated (purple). Blue alone measuring detection equals defensive.
A penetration test exploits; a vulnerability scan only identifies. If the question wants proof of impact, choose the penetration test.
videos.realWorld: SOC analysts are on the receiving end of penetration tests: a good SOC treats every engagement as a free detection exercise and reviews afterwards which of the tester's actions produced alerts and which did not. GRC analysts manage the programme: scheduling the annual tests that PCI DSS and the CBN expect, ensuring rules of engagement and authorisation letters are signed, tracking findings to remediation in the risk register, and confirming retests close the critical ones before the compliance deadline.

quiz.q: A bank hires a firm to test its internet banking application and provides the testers with a standard customer account and the application URL but no source code or architecture documents. Which type of test is this?
quiz.explain: Providing limited information such as a user account is a partially known environment test. A known environment would include full documentation and code; an unknown environment would provide nothing.

quiz.q: Before scanning any systems, a penetration tester reviews certificate transparency logs, WHOIS records, employee profiles on LinkedIn and public code repositories belonging to the target. Which activity is being performed?
quiz.explain: Gathering information from public sources without interacting with the target's systems is passive reconnaissance. Active reconnaissance involves scanning or probing the target, and the other options describe test postures, not discovery methods.

quiz.q: A fintech's SOC manager wants a test in which attackers run techniques while the SOC watches in real time, and detection rules are tuned immediately whenever a technique goes unnoticed. Which type of engagement fits this goal?
quiz.explain: An integrated test combines offensive and defensive teams working together to test and improve detection in real time. An offensive-only test would not include collaborative tuning, and the other options address different scopes.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, implement security awareness practices

videos.title: Security Awareness
videos.summary: Messer covers phishing campaigns, recognising and responding to phishing, anomalous behaviour recognition, and the reporting and monitoring that turn awareness into measurable results.
videos.deepDive:
Security awareness is the control that addresses the vulnerability every other control depends on: the person at the keyboard. Most breaches still begin with a human action: a clicked link, a reused password, a USB drive picked up in a car park, a call from someone claiming to be IT. Awareness does not make people perfect; its realistic goal is to make risky behaviour rarer and reporting faster, so the SOC hears about the phishing email at minute two rather than day five. ISO 27001 Annex A control 6.3 requires awareness education and training, the CBN framework requires banks to run awareness programmes for staff and customers, and the NDPA expects staff handling personal data to be trained, so this is a compliance item with measurable outcomes.

Phishing campaigns are the core practical exercise. The security team sends simulated phishing emails to staff and measures who opens, who clicks, who enters credentials and who reports. A good programme varies the lures (a fake HR payslip portal, a delivery notification, a message from the CEO asking for an urgent transfer, a vendor invoice), targets departments with realistic pretexts (finance gets invoice fraud, HR gets fake CVs with macros), and raises difficulty over time. The metrics are the point: click rate, credential submission rate, report rate and time-to-first-report, tracked per department and per quarter. A drop from 18 percent to 4 percent click rate over a year is the evidence you show the risk committee. Users who click are not punished on first offence; they get immediate, short, just-in-time training that explains what they missed. Repeat clickers get additional training and, in high-risk roles, may be escalated to their manager.

Recognising phishing is taught through concrete signals: mismatched sender domain (a look-alike domain with a swapped letter), urgency and threats, unexpected attachments, requests to bypass process, links whose hover text differs from the displayed text, generic greetings, and requests for credentials or payment changes. Responding is drilled as a single reflex: do not click, do not reply, use the report button, and if you already clicked, tell the SOC immediately because early reporting limits the damage and nobody is blamed for reporting. The report button in the mail client, wired to the SOC's phishing playbook from 5.1, is the single highest-value awareness tool a bank can deploy.

Anomalous behaviour recognition extends awareness beyond email. Staff are taught to notice and report three categories:

  • Risky behaviour: colleagues sharing passwords, disabling antivirus, plugging in unknown USB devices, emailing customer lists to personal accounts, propping open secure doors.
  • Unexpected behaviour: a system prompting for credentials it never asked for before, a workstation running slowly with high disk activity, MFA prompts arriving when the user did not log in (a sign of credential compromise and MFA fatigue attacks), files renamed with strange extensions.
  • Unintentional behaviour: honest mistakes such as sending a spreadsheet to the wrong recipient or misconfiguring a sharing link. The culture goal is that people self-report these quickly because the response to an honest report is help, not punishment.

Reporting and monitoring is the feedback loop. Initial reporting establishes the baseline: the first phishing simulation and the first survey show where the organisation starts. Recurring reporting tracks the trend: quarterly campaign results, training completion, report rates and the number of real incidents that began with a user report. These become KRIs in the risk register (phishing click rate above 5 percent triggers targeted training) and appear in the CISO's board pack. Monitoring also catches the silent problem of staff who never report anything, which usually means they do not know how.

Worked example: a bank's Q1 simulation sends a fake CBN circular attachment to 3,000 staff. 14 percent open the attachment, 6 percent enable macros, 22 percent report. The awareness lead runs targeted sessions for the two branches with the highest rates, adds a report button reminder to the intranet, and in Q2 a different lure produces 7 percent opens, 2 percent macro enablement and 41 percent reports. The GRC analyst records the trend against the KRI threshold and the SOC notes that the median time to first report fell from 3 hours to 12 minutes, which is the number that actually protects the bank.

keyTerms.def: The ongoing effort to make staff recognise threats and behave securely, measured by behaviour change rather than attendance.
A simulated phishing exercise sent to staff to measure click, credential submission and report rates and to deliver just-in-time training.
Brief training delivered at the moment a user makes a mistake, such as immediately after clicking a simulated phishing link.
The percentage of recipients who report a simulated or real phishing message, often the most valuable awareness metric.
User actions that knowingly or carelessly increase risk, such as sharing passwords or disabling security tools.
System or account activity the user did not initiate, such as unrequested MFA prompts, that may indicate compromise.
Honest user mistakes such as misdirected emails that should be reported quickly without fear of blame.
Establishing a baseline measurement of awareness and then tracking trends over repeated cycles.

examTips: If a scenario asks how to measure whether awareness training works, the answer is phishing simulation metrics tracked over time, not training attendance.
Unrequested MFA prompts are unexpected behaviour signalling credential compromise; the correct user response is to deny and report.
Users who fail a simulation get immediate targeted training; the exam does not favour punishment on a first failure.
Initial reporting sets the baseline; recurring reporting shows the trend. Questions about proving improvement point to recurring.
videos.realWorld: In most Nigerian banks the awareness programme is owned by the security governance or GRC team and delivered with the phishing simulation platform integrated into the mail system. The GRC analyst schedules campaigns, produces the departmental league table, and prepares the quarterly board metric. The SOC benefits directly: user reports through the phishing button are one of the top sources of real incidents, and the analysts triage them with the phishing playbook and feed the indicators back into the mail gateway and EDR blocklists.

quiz.q: A bank's CISO wants to demonstrate to the board that the awareness programme is reducing risk. Which metric best supports this?
options: The number of employees who attended the annual security talk
The trend in phishing simulation click rates and report rates over the last four quarters
The number of policies published on the intranet
The total cost of the awareness platform
quiz.explain: Behaviour change over time, shown by falling click rates and rising report rates across recurring simulations, demonstrates risk reduction. Attendance, publication counts and cost measure activity or spend, not effectiveness.

quiz.q: An employee receives several push notifications from the bank's MFA app asking to approve a login, although they have not attempted to log in. According to awareness training, what should the employee do?
options: Approve one notification to make them stop
Ignore them, since MFA is working as intended
Deny the requests and immediately report the unexpected activity to the security team
quiz.explain: Unrequested MFA prompts indicate that someone has the user's password and is attempting an MFA fatigue attack. The correct response is to deny and report so the SOC can reset credentials and investigate. Approving would grant the attacker access.

quiz.q: During a phishing simulation, 20 percent of staff in the operations department entered their credentials on the fake login page. What is the most appropriate immediate response?
options: Disable email for the operations department
Cancel the awareness programme as ineffective
Terminate the employees who entered credentials
Deliver immediate targeted training to those users and schedule a follow-up simulation to measure improvement
quiz.explain: Awareness programmes respond to failures with just-in-time targeted training and then re-measure. Termination on first failure, disabling email or abandoning the programme are disproportionate and do not reduce risk.

videos.title: User Training
videos.summary: Messer covers the content of user guidance and training (policies and handbooks, situational awareness, insider threat, password management, removable media and cables, social engineering, operational security, hybrid and remote work) and the development and execution of an awareness programme.
videos.deepDive:
User training is the delivery side of awareness: the actual content people learn and the programme that gets it to them. Security+ lists the topics a complete programme must cover and expects you to build and run one for a given scenario. The exam's 5.6 objective says given a scenario, implement, so questions describe a workplace situation and ask which training topic or programme step addresses it.

Core training content:

  • Policy and handbooks: every employee must know where the security policies live, what the AUP requires, and how to report incidents. The employee handbook summarises these in plain language, and onboarding includes an acknowledgement. Training here is not memorising the policy; it is knowing it exists and what it means for their job.
  • Situational awareness: noticing what is happening around you: an unfamiliar person in a restricted area, a screen left unlocked, a colleague under unusual pressure to make a payment, a login page that looks slightly wrong. It is the habit of pausing before acting.
  • Insider threat: recognising indicators that a colleague may be a risk: unusual access requests, downloading large volumes of data, working odd hours without reason, expressing grievances, bypassing controls. Training also covers the honest side: how to raise a concern confidentially, and why the organisation monitors privileged activity. In banks, insider fraud is a larger loss category than external hacking, so this module is taken seriously.
  • Password management: use of the approved password manager, unique passphrases per system, never sharing or reusing, enabling MFA, and recognising credential harvesting pages. Modern guidance emphasises length and uniqueness over forced complexity and rotation.
  • Removable media and cables: not plugging in found USB drives, using only approved encrypted media, and being aware that malicious cables and chargers exist that can inject keystrokes or exfiltrate data (the O.MG cable class of attack). Banks commonly block USB storage entirely and training explains why.
  • Social engineering: the full range beyond email: vishing calls impersonating the bank's IT desk or the CBN, smishing with fake account alerts, pretexting by fake vendors, tailgating, and business email compromise where a spoofed executive requests an urgent transfer. Training uses real examples and teaches verification through a known channel before acting.
  • Operational security (OPSEC): not disclosing internal details that help attackers: system names in social media posts, badge photos on LinkedIn, project details in public conversations, out-of-office replies naming who to contact and when the CFO is travelling.
  • Hybrid and remote work environments: securing the home network, using the VPN or zero-trust access, no work on public Wi-Fi without protection, screen privacy in public places, keeping family off work devices, locking screens, and physical security of laptops during transport. Since 2020 this is the module most in need of updating in many organisations.

Programme development follows a lifecycle. Assess: identify the audience groups (all staff, developers, finance, privileged administrators, executives, third-party contractors) and the risks specific to each. Design: choose content and formats per group: short e-learning modules for everyone, role-based sessions for developers on secure coding and for finance on payment fraud, tabletop exercises for executives, and simulations for all. Set objectives that are measurable: 95 percent completion within 30 days of hire, click rate below 5 percent, report rate above 30 percent. Secure sponsorship: an executive who visibly participates, because staff mirror leadership.

Execution covers delivery and continuous improvement. Onboarding training is completed before system access is granted. Annual refreshers are mandatory and tracked, with reminders and manager escalation for non-completion. Campaigns run continuously: monthly simulations, posters and intranet articles tied to current threats, and a security champions network of volunteers in each department who relay messages and gather feedback. Results feed the recurring reports from the previous video and the programme is revised annually against incident data: if the year's real incidents were dominated by vishing, next year's content shifts toward it.

Worked example: a fintech with 400 staff, 60 developers and 12 finance approvers. All staff: quarterly 10-minute modules and monthly phishing simulations. Developers: annual secure coding workshop plus OWASP Top 10 refresher when the SDLC policy changes. Finance approvers: a BEC tabletop every six months and a mandatory callback verification procedure. Executives: an annual incident tabletop with the SOC. Completion, simulation results and real incident sources are reported quarterly, and the programme's own KRI is the percentage of real incidents first detected by a user report.

keyTerms.def: The habit of noticing and questioning unusual people, activity or requests in one's surroundings before acting.
Risk from current or former employees, contractors or partners who misuse legitimate access, whether maliciously or negligently.
Protecting seemingly harmless information that adversaries could combine to plan an attack.
Manipulating people into performing actions or divulging information, through phishing, vishing, smishing, pretexting or tailgating.
A charging or data cable modified to inject keystrokes or exfiltrate data when connected to a device.
Training content tailored to the specific risks and responsibilities of a job function, such as developers or finance approvers.
A non-security employee who volunteers to promote security practices and relay concerns within their team.
Delivering awareness training through onboarding, recurring refreshers and campaigns, and tracking completion and outcomes.

examTips: Match the scenario to the training topic: found USB drive equals removable media, urgent transfer request equals social engineering or BEC, public Wi-Fi equals remote work, LinkedIn post about internal systems equals OPSEC.

Development is designing the programme (audiences, content, objectives); execution is delivering, tracking and improving it. Questions about who to train and on what are development; questions about completion tracking are execution.
Role-based training beats one-size-fits-all; if a scenario describes a specific group with specific risks, the answer is tailored training for that group.
Onboarding training should be completed before access is granted, and refreshers are recurring, typically annual.
videos.realWorld: GRC analysts in banks own the training completion tracker and chase the last 5 percent every year, because auditors and CBN examiners sample staff records and ask for evidence of completion dates. The most effective analysts also act as the bridge to the SOC: when the SOC sees a spike in vishing calls impersonating the IT help desk, the analyst turns it into a same-week awareness bulletin and adds a vishing scenario to the next simulation, which is what a continuously improving programme looks like in practice.

quiz.q: A finance officer at a fintech receives a WhatsApp message that appears to come from the CEO, asking for an urgent transfer to a new supplier before close of business. Which training topic most directly prepares the officer to handle this correctly?
options: Social engineering, with verification through a known channel
quiz.explain: An impersonated executive requesting an urgent payment is business email compromise, a social engineering attack. Training teaches verifying such requests through a known, separate channel before acting. The other topics do not address this scenario.

quiz.q: A bank is designing its awareness programme and must decide what developers, finance approvers and executives should each receive, and how success will be measured. Which phase of the programme does this describe?
quiz.explain: Identifying audiences, tailoring content and setting measurable objectives are programme development activities. Execution is delivery and tracking, and reporting phases measure results after delivery.

quiz.q: An employee posts a photo on social media showing their access badge and a whiteboard listing internal server names and an upcoming migration date. Which training topic addresses this behaviour?
quiz.explain: Disclosing seemingly harmless internal details such as badge designs, system names and schedules that an attacker could exploit is an operational security failure. The behaviour is careless rather than malicious, so insider threat is not the best fit, and the other options are unrelated.
